So I had my first big SaaS sale as CEO before I was even sure it was a SaaS company yet (more on that
here
). It wasn’t easy, but we closed our first $100k customer without any prior experience with enterprise software sales. How did we do it?
First, we knew we weren’t going for small customers. We wanted the Big Guys. But we also didn’t have enough leads or time to close very large deals. So what kind of deal could we go after? And how would we make money off them?
The answer became clear when we finally got into meetings at some of the largest tech companies in the world.  At IBM. At Google. At Facebook. Etc. etc.  They said No to us because they already had their own solutions, often built by third parties like Salesforce, NetSuite, HubSpot, etc. But … they told me if there were no other alternatives …
they’d buy from us
. That’s right. Even back then, in the early days, you still needed multiple vendors just to get anything done in IT and more. There was no vendor lock-in back then (well, almost none), and so folks would pick up whatever solution seemed best for each use case, even if it wasn’t part of a full stack.
We realized that meant we could sell ourselves as “Best Solution #2” — which is a tough place to be, but where most startups end up anyway. To win, however, we needed to understand one thing well:  the social contract between the buyer and seller. Once you understand that, magic can happen. Let me share two simple examples.

I've been doing SaaS for a while now. I started my first company in 1998—before the iPhone was even invented—and it just IPO'd recently. That's a long time ago. It took us over 17 years to get there. So what have we learned along the way? What do you need to know as founders? And how does that apply to selling to CIOs?
Let me start with something that might surprise you. When I went to my first big tech conference, which was a trade show called PC Expo back then, but now is called Big Tech West—I went down on the last day when everyone had left and set up a booth for our little startup because I didn't want to pay money to rent one. At least I could save some cash by setting up myself. We got like six leads that day. All of them said exactly the same thing: "We're all looking for startups."
So if you're a founder listening right now and thinking, "Oh man, no one wants to buy from startups," actually they do. They love buying from startups. But only under very specific circumstances. Let me tell you those circumstances and why.
First let me share another story. A few months ago, I met the head of product engineering at Snowflake at a dinner party. He used to work at Salesforce.com. This guy literally built Appforce, the core platform behind Salesforce. Here he is building his own AI agent. How many people can build their own agentic app right now? Two. Maybe three. Me, him, two other guys. These two dudes. Building agents at scale. But here's what really impressed me. After being at Salesforce for almost a decade—he came back and worked at Slack for a year before coming to Snowflake—he told me, "This is so much easier than Salesforce." Why? Because the product velocity is insane. In the old days, Salesforce would release maybe five major features per quarter. Today, Snowflake releases 10 major new products every single week.
